subject: CREATIVE ARTS
title: Athletics
overview: Sprints are short, very fast races such as the 100 metres. In this sub-strand you will learn two ways of starting a sprint, the medium start and the elongated start, and how to run fast with good body posture. You will also sketch and paint the Kenyan flag, fix it on a handle and use it to cheer your classmates, and talk about why the flag is flown at athletics events.

lessons.title: The crouch start: medium and elongated sprint starts
objectives: Describe what a runner does at the commands “On your marks”, “Set” and “Go”.
Tell the difference between a medium start and an elongated start.
Get into the medium and elongated start positions.
lessons.intro: In a short race, a good start can win or lose the race. Sprinters do not start standing up. They crouch low behind the starting line so that they can push off quickly when the race begins.
lessons.notes:
A sprint is a short race run at top speed from start to finish. Sprinters use a crouch start, which means they begin low down with their hands on the ground. The starter gives three signals.

### 1. “On your marks”
- Walk up to the starting line and stand in your own lane.
- Place your hands just behind the line, a little wider than your shoulders. Make a bridge with your thumb and fingers; do not touch the line.
- Put your stronger foot in front and kneel on the knee of your back leg.
- Keep your arms straight, your head relaxed and your eyes looking at the ground a short distance ahead.

### 2. “Set”
- Lift your hips until they are a little higher than your shoulders.
- Move your weight forward onto your hands and your front leg.
- Stay completely still. Moving now is a false start.

### 3. “Go” (or the whistle, clapper or gun)
- Push hard with both feet and drive your arms.
- The back leg comes forward first.
- Stay low for the first few strides, then rise slowly into your running position.

### Medium start and elongated start
The two starts differ in how far apart the feet are when you kneel at “On your marks”.

- **Medium start:** the knee of the back leg is opposite the middle of the front foot. The feet are a medium distance apart.
- **Elongated start:** the knee of the back leg is level with, or just behind, the heel of the front foot. The feet are further apart, so the body is stretched out (elongated means stretched long).

Try both starts and find out which one helps you push off strongly and keep your balance. A good start position is steady, balanced and comfortable.

keyWords.meaning: a short race run at full speed
a start in which the runner begins low with hands on the ground
moving or leaving the start before the signal to go
stretched long

examples.problem: Wanjiru kneels at the start. Her back knee is level with the heel of her front foot. Which start is she using?
steps: In the medium start the back knee is opposite the middle of the front foot.
In the elongated start the back knee is level with or behind the front heel.

examples.problem: Otieno moves forward when the starter says “Set”. What has he done?
steps: At “Set” the runner must stay still.
Moving before the signal to go is not allowed.
examples.answer: He has made a false start.

activity.title: Practising the two starts
materials: Open field or track with a marked starting line
Digital device with a video of sprint starts (if available)
steps: Watch a live or video demonstration of a crouch start and name the three commands.
In pairs, get into the medium start position while your partner checks where your back knee is.
Swap roles, then practise the elongated start in the same way.
On the whistle, push off and run 10 to 15 metres, staying low for the first few steps.
Tell your partner which start felt steadier for you and why.

practice.question: Name the three signals a starter gives in a sprint race.
practice.answer: On your marks, Set, Go (or the whistle, clapper or gun).

practice.question: Where is the back knee in a medium start?
practice.answer: Opposite the middle of the front foot.

practice.question: What should you do with your hips at the command “Set”?
practice.answer: Lift them until they are a little higher than the shoulders and stay still.

practice.question: Why should your hands not touch the starting line?
practice.answer: Touching or crossing the line is not allowed; the hands must be just behind it.

summary: Sprinters use a crouch start with three signals: On your marks, Set, Go.
In the medium start the back knee is opposite the middle of the front foot.
In the elongated start the back knee is level with or behind the front heel.

lessons.title: Sprinting technique and posture
objectives: Describe the correct body posture for sprinting.
Run a short sprint using correct arm and leg action.
Explain why good posture matters in a sprint.
lessons.intro: Two learners can be equally strong, but the one who runs with good form usually wins. How you hold your head, arms and body decides how much of your energy pushes you forward.
lessons.notes:
After the start, a sprinter must reach top speed quickly and keep it until the finish line. The way you move your body is called your sprinting technique.

### Head and body
- Keep your head still and look straight ahead down your lane.
- Lean your body slightly forward, with your back straight, not bent.
- Keep your face, neck and shoulders relaxed. A tight body slows you down.

### Arms
- Bend your elbows at about a right angle (like the corner of a book).
- Swing your arms forwards and backwards, not across your body.
- Your hands come up to about chin height in front and back past your hip behind.
- Fast arms help you get fast legs.

### Legs and feet
- Run on the balls of your feet (the front part of the foot), not on your heels.
- Lift your knees high in front of you.
- Push off strongly from the ground with each stride.

### The finish
- Keep running at full speed through the finish line; do not slow down before it.
- Lean your chest forward as you cross the line.
- Slow down gradually after the line and stay in your lane.

### Why posture matters
Good posture keeps your body balanced so that all your effort pushes you forward. Swinging arms across the body or leaning back makes the body twist and wastes energy. Looking sideways at other runners can make you slow down or leave your lane.

### Safety
Warm up before sprinting, run only in your own lane, wear suitable shoes or run on a surface without stones and thorns, and cool down after running.

keyWords.meaning: the way you hold your body
the padded front part of the foot just behind the toes
the marked strip of the track in which one runner must stay
one long running step

examples.problem: Kiprono swings his arms across his chest while sprinting. How should he correct this?
steps: Arms should swing forwards and backwards.
Crossing the body makes the body twist and wastes energy.
examples.answer: He should bend his elbows and swing his arms forwards and backwards beside his body.

examples.problem: Amina slows down just before the finish line. What should she do instead?
steps: A sprinter runs at full speed through the line.
She leans her chest forward as she crosses.
examples.answer: Keep running at full speed through the line and lean her chest forward.

activity.title: Sprint form drills
materials: Cones or stones to mark distances
steps: Warm up by jogging slowly around the field and stretching.
Stand still and practise the arm swing for 20 counts while a partner checks your elbows.
March on the spot lifting your knees high, then jog doing the same.
Run 30 metres at full speed, focusing on looking ahead and running on the balls of your feet.
Your partner watches and tells you one thing you did well and one thing to improve.

practice.question: Which part of the foot should a sprinter run on?
practice.answer: The balls of the feet.

practice.question: In which direction should a sprinter swing the arms?
practice.answer: Forwards and backwards, not across the body.

practice.question: Why is it important to maintain appropriate posture during sprints?
practice.answer: It keeps the body balanced so that energy pushes the runner forward, helping the runner go faster and avoid falling or leaving the lane.

summary: Look ahead, lean slightly forward and stay relaxed.
Bend the elbows and swing the arms forwards and backwards.
Run on the balls of the feet with high knees and run through the finish line.

lessons.title: Sketching and painting the Kenyan flag
objectives: Sketch the Kenyan flag with its stripes, shield and spears in the correct order.
Paint the flag neatly using the correct colours.
Attach the flag to a handle.
lessons.intro: At athletics meetings, supporters wave Kenyan flags to cheer the runners. In this lesson you will make your own flag to wave during your class sprint races.
lessons.notes:
The Kenyan flag is a rectangle. Its length is one and a half times its height (the ratio of height to length is 2 : 3). It has five stripes that run across the flag from side to side.

### Colour arrangement from top to bottom
1. Black (a wide stripe)
2. White (a thin stripe)
3. Red (a wide stripe)
4. White (a thin stripe)
5. Green (a wide stripe)

In the centre there is a red, black and white Maasai shield with two white spears crossed behind it.

### What the colours stand for
- Black stands for the people of Kenya.
- Red stands for the blood shed during the struggle for independence.
- Green stands for agriculture and the natural resources of the land.
- White stands for peace and unity.
- The shield and spears stand for the defence of freedom.

### Steps for sketching
1. Draw a rectangle lightly in pencil. For example, make it 15 cm long and 10 cm high.
2. Divide the height into three wide stripes with two thin stripes between them.
3. Draw the shield as an upright oval shape in the centre, with two crossed spears behind it so that the tips show above and the ends show below.

### Steps for painting
1. Paint one colour at a time, starting with the lightest. Leave the white stripes as the white of the paper or fabric if your material is white.
2. Let each colour dry before painting the colour next to it, so that the colours do not run into each other.
3. Use a thin brush for the shield and spears and a wider brush for the stripes.
4. Keep inside the pencil lines for neat edges.

### Attaching a handle
When the paint is dry, fold the left edge of the flag around a smooth stick or rolled paper and glue or tape it firmly. Check that the black stripe is at the top when you hold the stick upright on the left.

keyWords.meaning: a light, quick drawing that shows the main shapes
the order in which the colours are placed
cloth

examples.problem: Juma painted his flag with green at the top and black at the bottom. What is wrong?
steps: The correct order from the top is black, white, red, white, green.
examples.answer: The order is upside down; black should be at the top and green at the bottom.

examples.problem: Your flag is 12 cm high. How long should it be?
steps: The length is one and a half times the height.
Half of 12 is 6, and 12 + 6 = 18.

activity.title: Make a cheering flag
materials: Black, red and green paint or crayons
Stick or rolled paper for the handle
steps: Sketch the flag lightly in pencil using a ruler for the stripes.
Check the colour arrangement with a partner before painting.
Paint the flag neatly, letting each colour dry before painting the next.
Attach the flag to a handle.
Keep your flag for cheering during the class sprint races.

practice.question: List the colours of the Kenyan flag from top to bottom.
practice.answer: Black, white, red, white, green.

practice.question: What is in the centre of the Kenyan flag?
practice.answer: A Maasai shield with two crossed white spears.

practice.question: What does the green colour stand for?
practice.answer: Agriculture and the natural resources of the land.

practice.question: Why should you let one colour dry before painting the next one?
practice.answer: So that the wet colours do not run into each other and the flag stays neat.

summary: The Kenyan flag has black, white, red, white and green stripes from top to bottom.
A shield and two crossed spears are in the centre.
Sketch first, paint one colour at a time, then attach a handle.

lessons.title: Sprint races and flying the Kenyan flag
objectives: Run a sprint race using a crouch start and good sprinting technique.
Explain why the Kenyan flag is flown during athletics events.
Cheer others safely using the flags made.
lessons.intro: When a Kenyan athlete wins a race at a big championship, the Kenyan flag is raised and many athletes run around the track carrying it. The flag shows the world which country the winner comes from.
lessons.notes:
In this lesson you put your start and sprinting skills together in real races, and you use the flags you made to cheer.

### Running a class sprint race
- The class is divided into small groups, one runner for each lane.
- The starter stands where all runners can see or hear the signal.
- Runners use the medium or elongated crouch start.
- Judges stand at the finish line to see who crosses first.
- Runners stay in their own lanes all the way and slow down gently after the finish.

### Why the national flag is flown at athletics events
- **Identity:** the flag shows which country an athlete represents.
- **Patriotism:** waving the flag shows love and pride for our country.
- **Encouragement:** seeing the flag in the crowd gives athletes strength to run harder.
- **Unity:** people from all communities cheer together under one flag.
- **Honour:** when a country's athlete wins a medal at a big championship, that country's flag is raised.

The flag should be treated with respect. Do not let it drag on the ground, do not step on it and do not use it to hit others. Hold it upright and wave it above your head or to the side.

### Cheering safely
- Stand behind the lines, not on the track.
- Wave flags where they do not block the runners or hit other people.
- Cheer every runner, not only your friends. Clapping and kind words are part of good sportsmanship.

After the races, talk about what helped the fastest runners: a steady start, arms swinging forwards and backwards, looking ahead and running through the line.

keyWords.meaning: love for and pride in one's country
to stand for or take part on behalf of a group or country
playing fairly and treating others kindly in games

examples.problem: Why might an athlete run around the track holding the national flag after winning?
steps: The flag shows the country the athlete represents.
It shows pride and thanks to the country.
examples.answer: To show the country they represent and their pride in their country.

activity.title: Class sprint championship
materials: Marked track or field with lanes
steps: Warm up together as a class.
Take turns as runners, starter, judges and cheering supporters.
Run a 50-metre sprint using a crouch start of your choice.
Supporters wave their flags safely behind the lines and cheer every runner.
After the races, discuss in groups why the national flag is flown at athletics events.

practice.question: Give two reasons why the national flag is flown during a national athletics event.
practice.answer: Any two: to show the country the athletes represent, to show patriotism, to encourage athletes, to unite the fans, to honour a winner.

practice.question: Name two ways of showing respect for the flag.
practice.answer: Any two: do not let it touch the ground, do not step on it, hold it upright, do not use it to hit others.

practice.question: Where should supporters stand while cheering during a race?
practice.answer: Behind the lines, off the track, where they do not block the runners.

summary: A sprint race needs a starter, runners in lanes and judges at the finish.
The flag shows identity, patriotism and unity and encourages athletes.
Cheer every runner safely and treat the flag with respect.

lessons.title: Warming up, cooling down and sprint safety
objectives: Lead a simple warm-up and cool-down for sprinting.
State safety rules for sprinting on the field or track.
Explain how a warm-up protects the body.
lessons.intro: A sprinter who starts a race with cold, stiff muscles can pull a muscle before the race is even interesting. Preparing the body is part of sprinting technique.
lessons.notes:
A warm-up is a set of easy movements done before hard running. It raises the heart rate slowly, warms the muscles and reminds the body of the posture you will use in the race. A cool-down is the easy movement done after the race so the heart can slow down gently.

### A warm-up you can lead
1. Jog slowly around the field for about two minutes.
2. March on the spot and lift the knees to hip height.
3. Circle the arms forwards ten times, then backwards ten times.
4. Do ten easy squats, keeping the heels down.
5. Run three short bursts of about ten metres at half speed, then walk back.

Keep the shoulders relaxed and the eyes forward even during the jog. The posture you practise slowly is the posture you want when you sprint.

### A cool-down
Walk for about two minutes. Then stretch the back of each leg and the front of each thigh. Hold a stretch still. Do not bounce. Breathe out slowly. Shaking the arms and legs also helps the body settle.

### Safety on the sprint area
- Walk the ground first and remove stones, sticks and anything that can cut the feet.
- Wear shoes that fit, or run barefoot only on smooth grass the teacher has checked.
- Tie long hair back and empty pockets of pens and sharp objects.
- Give each runner a clear lane and run in one direction.
- Stop at once if you feel a sharp pain, dizziness or sickness, and tell the teacher.
- Drink water before and after running. Do not take huge gulps in the middle of a sprint.

Safety is part of skill. A fast runner who crashes into a friend or trips on a stone has not performed the sprint well. Look after yourself and the people in the lanes beside you.

keyWords.meaning: easy movements done before hard exercise to prepare the body
easy movements done after exercise so the body can settle
an injury caused by forcing a muscle that is not ready

examples.problem: Halima wants to sprint as soon as she arrives on the field. What should she do first, and why?
steps: Hard running needs warm muscles.
A warm-up raises the heart rate slowly and prepares the joints.
examples.answer: She should warm up first so her muscles are ready and she is less likely to strain them.

examples.problem: After the race, Baraka stops suddenly and sits down. What is a better cool-down?
steps: The heart should slow down gradually.
Walking and still stretches help the body settle.
examples.answer: Walk for about two minutes, then hold still stretches without bouncing.

activity.title: Lead a sprint warm-up
materials: Water to drink after the session
steps: In groups of four, one learner leads the five-part warm-up while the others follow.
Check the ground together and agree one safety rule your group will keep.
Practise three easy accelerations of about ten metres.
Swap the leader and repeat.
Cool down with a walk and two stretches, and tell the group how your body feels.

practice.question: Give two parts of a sprint warm-up.
practice.answer: Any two: slow jogging, high-knee marching, arm circles, easy squats, short half-speed runs.

practice.question: Why do you hold a stretch still instead of bouncing?
practice.answer: Bouncing can strain a muscle. A still stretch is safer.

practice.question: Name two safety checks before a sprint lesson.
practice.answer: Any two: clear the ground, wear suitable shoes, tie hair, empty pockets, give each runner a lane, have water ready.

summary: Warm up before sprinting and cool down afterwards.
Check the ground, your clothing and the space around other runners.
Stop and tell the teacher if you feel pain or dizziness.

lessons.title: The drive: first strides after the start
objectives: Describe how the body leaves the crouch start.
Run the first strides low and strong before rising.
Correct the mistake of standing up too soon.
lessons.intro: The race is often decided in the first few steps. A strong push from the crouch start builds speed. Standing up too soon wastes that push.
lessons.notes:
The moment after the signal to go is called the drive. In the drive the runner stays low and pushes the ground hard to build speed. This building of speed is also called acceleration.

### What the body does
- Both feet push the ground. The back leg then swings forward quickly.
- The arms drive as strongly as the legs: one elbow forward, one elbow back. The hands do not cross the middle of the body.
- The first strides are shorter and more powerful than the strides later in the race.
- The chest rises a little with each stride. The runner does not jump straight up on the first step.
- The eyes look a few metres ahead at first, then further down the lane as the body comes upright.
- After about ten to fifteen metres the runner is tall and sprinting: high knees, balls of the feet, relaxed face.

### A common mistake
Many beginners hear “Go” and pop upright at once, as if they were answering a question in class. The body then has nothing to push against, and the first steps are slow. If a partner sees your head shoot up, practise the start again and think “push the ground, stay low”.

### A practice pattern
From your chosen crouch start, drive for five strides only, then walk. Repeat. When the five strides stay low and straight, add a longer run of about twenty metres and rise smoothly into full sprinting technique.

The drive works from both the medium start and the elongated start. The start position gets you ready. The drive turns that position into speed.

keyWords.meaning: the strong, low push out of the start that builds speed
getting faster
one running step

examples.problem: On “Go”, Nekesa stands fully upright on her first step. What should she change?
steps: The first strides should stay low.
She should push the ground and let the chest rise gradually.
examples.answer: She should stay low for the first strides and rise little by little.

examples.problem: A runner drives for about 12 metres before sprinting upright. Is that a reasonable drive distance?
steps: The drive lasts about ten to fifteen metres.
12 is between 10 and 15.
examples.answer: Yes. About ten to fifteen metres is a suitable drive before the upright sprint.

activity.title: Five-stride drives
materials: Marked lane or a line on the field
steps: Warm up, then take your medium or elongated start.
On the whistle, drive for five strides only and freeze.
Your partner says whether you stayed low or stood up too soon.
Repeat three times, then run about twenty metres, rising smoothly.
Swap roles.

practice.question: What is the drive in a sprint?
practice.answer: The strong, low push out of the start that builds speed.

practice.question: Should the first strides be long and upright, or shorter and low?
practice.answer: Shorter and low.

practice.question: About how far does the drive last before the runner is upright?
practice.answer: About ten to fifteen metres.

summary: Push the ground and stay low for the first strides.
Let the body rise gradually over about ten to fifteen metres.
Arms drive forwards and backwards with the legs.

lessons.title: Comparing the medium and elongated starts
objectives: Show the foot and knee positions of both sprint starts.
Choose the start you can hold still and push from.
Practise both starts over a short distance.
lessons.intro: Two correct crouch starts do not feel the same. One packs the feet closer together. The other stretches the body longer. You need to know both and choose the one that keeps you balanced.
lessons.notes:
Both the medium start and the elongated start are crouch starts. You still wait for “On your marks”, “Set” and “Go”. You still keep your hands just behind the line and your fingers bridged. The difference is the distance between the feet.

### Medium start
Kneel so that the knee of the back leg is beside the middle of the front foot. The feet are a comfortable, middle distance apart. Many runners find the first step feels quick because the back foot is not too far away. If you are shorter, or if the elongated start makes you wobble, the medium start is often easier to balance.

### Elongated start
Kneel so that the back knee is level with the heel of the front foot, or just behind that heel. Elongated means stretched long, so the body covers more ground before you move. The push can feel strong. Taller runners sometimes prefer it. If your hips collapse or your hands slip, the feet are too far apart and you should shorten the position.

### How to choose
A good start is the one you can hold perfectly still at “Set” and push from without falling forward or sitting back. Try this test with a partner:

1. Do three medium starts and run about fifteen metres.
2. Do three elongated starts over the same distance.
3. Your partner checks only the back knee: middle of the front foot, or by the heel.
4. Say which start felt steadier. Use that one in the next race, but keep practising both so you can explain them.

Neither start allows a false start. However comfortable the position feels, you wait for the signal.

keyWords.meaning: a crouch start with the back knee beside the middle of the front foot
a crouch start with the feet further apart and the back knee by the front heel
a steady body that is not falling forward or backwards

examples.problem: Cherono’s back knee is beside the middle of her front foot. Which start is this?
steps: Middle of the front foot matches the medium start.
The heel matches the elongated start.

examples.problem: In the elongated start, Kamau’s hands keep slipping and his hips drop. What should he try?
steps: Slipping and dropping hips can mean the feet are too far apart.
He can shorten the position toward a medium start.
examples.answer: Bring the feet a little closer and try the medium start so he can balance.

activity.title: Test both starts
steps: Watch a demonstration or a short video of both starts again if one is available.
Practise the medium start three times over fifteen metres while a partner checks your back knee.
Practise the elongated start three times in the same way.
Tell your partner which start you could hold still, and which push felt stronger.
Run one more fifteen metres with the start you chose.

practice.question: Where is the back knee in the elongated start?
practice.answer: Level with, or just behind, the heel of the front foot.

practice.question: Where is the back knee in the medium start?
practice.answer: Beside the middle of the front foot.

practice.question: What makes a start the right choice for you?
practice.answer: You can hold it still at “Set” and push off without falling forward or sitting back.

practice.question: Are the commands different for the two starts?
practice.answer: No. Both use On your marks, Set and Go.

summary: Medium start: back knee by the middle of the front foot.
Elongated start: back knee by the front heel, body stretched longer.
Choose the start you can hold still and push from safely.

lessons.title: A class sprint meeting
objectives: Carry out a role in a class sprint race.
Run using a crouch start, a low drive and upright sprinting.
Cheer with the Kenyan flag and explain why it is flown.
lessons.intro: A real athletics meeting needs more than fast legs. It needs a starter, judges, a safe track and people who know how to honour the flag. Your class can run a small meeting that uses every skill in this sub-strand.
lessons.notes:
Put the skills together in a short meeting. Each learner runs, and each learner also serves the meeting in another role.

### Roles
- **Starter:** gives “On your marks”, “Set” and the whistle. Watches for anyone who moves early.
- **Runners:** use the medium or elongated start, drive low, then sprint upright in their own lanes through the finish.
- **Finish judges:** stand in line with the finish, off the track, and agree who crossed first. They watch the chest, not the arms.
- **Supporters:** stand well behind the lines and wave the flags they painted. They cheer every runner.
- **Recorder:** writes the order of finish, 1st, 2nd and 3rd, so the class can see the results fairly.

### Fair play
Stay in your lane. Do not push. Wait for the signal. If you false-start, go back without arguing. After the race, clap the other runners. Winning is enjoyable, and so is racing honestly.

### The flag at the meeting
Hold the stick so that black is at the top and the flag does not touch the ground. Wave it beside the track, never across a runner’s path. The national flag is flown at an athletics event because it shows which country the athletes represent, it expresses patriotism, it encourages the runners, it unites the crowd and it honours a winner when a national flag is raised. Treating your class flag with care is practice for that respect.

Talk afterwards about what made the fastest runs work: a still “Set”, a low drive, arms going straight, and eyes on the lane.

keyWords.meaning: a person who watches the finish line and decides the order of the runners
competing honestly and treating other runners with respect
the person who writes down the results

examples.problem: Three runners finish. The recorder writes Akinyi 1st, Mutiso 2nd and Cherono 3rd. Who crossed the line before Mutiso?
steps: 1st comes before 2nd.
Akinyi is 1st.

examples.problem: A supporter steps onto the track to wave a flag at a runner. What is wrong?
steps: Supporters must stay off the track.
A flag must not get in a runner’s way.
examples.answer: The supporter is blocking the race. Supporters stay behind the lines and wave flags safely.

activity.title: Run the class sprint meeting
materials: Marked lanes and a finish line
steps: Warm up as a class and check the ground.
Give every learner a role: runner, starter, judge, supporter or recorder. Rotate so everyone runs.
Run a sprint of about 40 to 50 metres using a crouch start.
Supporters cheer with flags from behind the lines.
Record the order, clap all runners, cool down, and discuss why the national flag is flown at athletics events.

practice.question: What do finish judges watch for at the line?
practice.answer: Whose chest crosses the finish line first.

practice.question: Give two duties of supporters at a sprint race.
practice.answer: Stay off the track and cheer every runner, waving flags safely.

practice.question: Give two reasons the national flag is flown at an athletics event.
practice.answer: Any two: to show the country, to express patriotism, to encourage athletes, to unite people, to honour a winner.

summary: A sprint meeting needs runners, a starter, judges, supporters and a recorder.
Race in your lane, through the finish, and treat other runners fairly.
Wave the flag with respect, off the track, with black at the top.

quiz.question: In which start is the back knee level with or just behind the heel of the front foot?
quiz.explanation: Elongated means stretched; the feet are furthest apart in this start.

quiz.question: Where is the back knee in the medium start?
options: Opposite the middle of the front foot
Ahead of the toes of the front foot
quiz.explanation: In the medium start the back knee is opposite the middle of the front foot.

quiz.question: What should a runner do at the command “Set”?
options: Lift the hips a little higher than the shoulders and stay still
quiz.explanation: At “Set” the hips rise and the runner stays still until the signal to go.

quiz.question: Which is correct sprinting technique?
options: Running on the balls of the feet
quiz.explanation: Sprinters run on the balls of their feet with high knees.

quiz.question: What is a false start?
quiz.answer: Moving or leaving the start before the signal to go.
quiz.explanation: Runners must stay still at “Set” until the signal.

quiz.question: What should a sprinter do at the finish line?
options: Run through it at full speed and lean the chest forward
quiz.explanation: Slowing before the line loses time; lean the chest forward as you cross.

quiz.question: Which colour is at the top of the Kenyan flag?
quiz.explanation: From top to bottom: black, white, red, white, green.

quiz.question: Why should you let one colour dry before painting the next?
quiz.answer: So that the colours do not run into each other and the flag is neat.
quiz.explanation: Neatness is part of painting the flag well.

quiz.question: What does the white colour on the Kenyan flag stand for?
quiz.explanation: White stands for peace and unity.

quiz.question: Give one reason for flying the Kenyan flag during an athletics event.
quiz.answer: Any one: to show the country the athletes represent, to show patriotism, to encourage the athletes, to unite fans.
quiz.explanation: The flag is a symbol of the nation and brings people together.

sources: KICD Grade 4 Creative Arts Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Performing and Displaying, Sub-strand 2.1 Athletics
